In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\mathcal F:M\times S\to N$ be a smooth family of maps and let $Z\subseteq N$
be an embedded submanifold. If $\mathcal F\pitchfork Z$, then the set of
parameters $s\in S$ for which the slice $\mathcal F_s:M\to N$ fails to be
transverse to $Z$ is a null subset of $S$.

Let $F:M\to N$ be smooth, and let $Z\subseteq N$ be an embedded submanifold.
Then $F$ is **transverse to $Z$**, written $F\pitchfork Z$, when for every
$p\in F^{-1}(Z)$,

$$dF_p(T_pM)+T_{F(p)}Z=T_{F(p)}N.$$

If $F(M)\cap Z=\varnothing$, this condition is vacuous, so $F\pitchfork Z$
still holds.

If $F:M\to N$ is a submersion, then $F\pitchfork Z$ for every embedded
submanifold $Z\subseteq N$.

Let $M$, $S$, and $N$ be smooth manifolds. A **smooth family of maps from $M$
to $N$ parametrized by $S$** is a smooth map

$$\mathcal F:M\times S\to N.$$

For each $s\in S$, its **slice map** is

$$\mathcal F_s:M\to N,\qquad \mathcal F_s(p):=\mathcal F(p,s).$$

The map $\mathcal F$ itself is the **evaluation map** of the family.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $f:M\to N$ be smooth. Then there exist an open ball
$$ B\subseteq\mathbb R^m $$
containing $0$ and a smooth family of maps
$$ \mathcal F:M\times B\to N $$
such that $\mathcal F_0=f$ and, for every $p\in M$, the parameter map
$$ \mathcal F_p:B\to N,\qquad a\longmapsto \mathcal F(p,a), $$
is a submersion. In particular, the evaluation map $\mathcal F$ is a
submersion, so it is transverse to every closed embedded submanifold
$Z\subseteq N$.
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every open cover of a smooth manifold admits a smooth partition of unity subordinate to it.

Assume countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $F:M\to N$ be continuous, let $A\subseteq M$ be closed, and suppose $F$ is smooth on an open neighbourhood of $A$. Then there exist a smooth map $\widetilde F:M\to N$ and an open neighbourhood $W$ of $A$ such that $\widetilde F=F$ on $W$ and $F$ is homotopic to $\widetilde F$ by a homotopy fixed on $W$, hence relative to $A$. No compactness of $A$ or its neighbourhood is assumed.

Let $M$ be a smooth $m$-manifold, and let $\mathcal A$ be a smooth atlas on
$M$. A subset $A\subseteq M$ is **$\mathcal A$-null** when, for every chart
$(U,\varphi)\in\mathcal A$, the set

$$\varphi(A\cap U)\subseteq\mathbb R^m$$

is null in the Euclidean sense of [[def-null-and-content-zero-in-rn]] when
$m\ge 1$, and is empty when $m=0$. Equivalently, on a $0$-manifold the only
null subset is the empty set.

Under the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), the next proposition shows that this
condition is independent of the chosen smooth atlas. Under that premise one
may therefore speak simply of a **null subset of $M$**.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Every subset of a manifold null set is
null, and every countable union of manifold null sets is null.

Let $M$ be a positive-dimensional smooth manifold, let $\mathcal A$ be a smooth
atlas on $M$, and let $E\subseteq M$ be $\mathcal A$-null in the sense of
[[def-null-subset-of-a-smooth-manifold]]. Then $M\setminus E$ is dense in $M$.
In particular, under Countable Choice the conclusion holds for any manifold-null
set $E$.

Let $X$ be a classical algebraic variety over $\mathbb C$ in the sense of
[[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]]: a separated
quasi-compact locally ringed space over $\mathbb C$ with a finite cover by
affine models $Z\subseteq\mathbb C^n$, the morphisms being the regular maps,
i.e. the morphisms of locally ringed spaces over $\mathbb C$
([[def-morphism-locally-ringed-spaces]]).

(a) **Analytic topology.** An affine model $Z\subseteq\mathbb C^n$ carries the
subspace topology of the Euclidean topology of $\mathbb C^n$
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-metric-topology]],
[[rem-complex-euclidean-space-dictionary]],
[[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]). If $Z_1,Z_2\subseteq X$ are affine
models and $\varphi:Z_1\to Z_2$ is the structure-sheaf isomorphism, then on
$Z_1\cap Z_2$ the maps $\varphi$ and $\varphi^{-1}$ are given locally by
polynomial quotient functions
([[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]]) and are
therefore continuous for the Euclidean topologies: polynomial functions are
continuous, and a quotient is continuous wherever its denominator does not
vanish ([[lem-algebra-of-continuous-real-maps-on-a-space]],
[[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]]). Hence the topologies transported
from the two affine models agree on the overlap, so the affine-model topologies
glue to a unique topology on the underlying set of $X$
([[def-topological-space]], [[def-subspace-topology-top]]): the **analytic
topology** of $X$. Every regular map of complex classical varieties is
continuous for the analytic topologies, by the same local description
([[def-continuous-map-top]]), and the analytic topology refines the Zariski
topology because polynomial zero sets are Euclidean closed. Whenever a complex
algebraic variety is used as a topological space below it carries the analytic
topology, and each subvariety carries the subspace topology.

(b) **Smooth points.** Let $S$ be a classical variety over $\mathbb C$ and let
$x\in S$. The point $x$ is a **smooth point of $S$** if its algebraic local ring
$\mathcal O_{S,x}$ is a regular local ring: a nonzero Noetherian local ring
whose maximal ideal $\mathfrak m_x$ satisfies
$\dim_{\mathbb C}(\mathfrak m_x/\mathfrak m_x^2)=\dim\mathcal O_{S,x}$
([[def-embedding-dimension-and-regular-local-ring]]). The residue field at a
classical complex point is $\mathbb C$. The variety $S$ is **smooth** if every
point is smooth. This intrinsic algebraic condition does not require a Zariski
neighbourhood to be algebraically isomorphic to an open subset of affine space.

(c) **Finite smooth algebraic stratifications.** A **finite smooth algebraic
stratification with the frontier condition** of $X$ is a finite decomposition
$X=\coprod_{\alpha\in A}S_\alpha$ into pairwise disjoint nonempty connected
locally closed subsets $S_\alpha\subseteq X$ — the **strata** — such that each
$S_\alpha$, with its reduced induced algebraic structure, is a smooth algebraic
subvariety of $X$; and such that for every $\alpha$ the closure
$\overline{S_\alpha}$ of $S_\alpha$ in $X$ is a union of strata. The latter is
the **frontier condition**: the frontier
$\overline{S_\alpha}\setminus S_\alpha$ of every stratum is a union of strata
([[def-connected-space]], [[def-interior-closure-boundary-top]]).

**The induced structure is the polynomial-quotient function sheaf, not a
restriction of $\mathcal O_X$.** A locally closed $S\subseteq X$ is, locally
inside an affine model $Z\subseteq\mathbb C^n$, the set of points with $h\neq0$
and $f_1=\dots=f_r=0$ for polynomials $h,f_1,\dots,f_r$ on $Z$
([[def-constructible-subset-variety]],
[[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]]); the map
$z\mapsto(z,1/h(z))$ identifies it with the affine model
$\{(z,t):th(z)=1,\ f_1(z)=\dots=f_r(z)=0\}\subseteq\mathbb C^{n+1}$, and its
**reduced induced structure sheaf** is the one transported along this
identification: locally functions of the form $a/b$ with $b$ nonvanishing on the
set. The ambient restriction $\mathcal O_X|_S$ is not used, since already at the
origin of the affine line the ambient stalk is the local ring of the line while
the stalk of the reduced point is $\mathbb C$. An open subset of an affine model
is a union of principal open subsets, and each principal open subset is again an
affine model, so every locally closed subvariety of $X$ is a classical variety
for the induced structure sheaf. No existence theorem for stratifications, no
common-refinement theorem and no choice principle is asserted: nothing is
selected, and all cited suppliers are choice-free.

Assume the Axiom of Choice (AC). Let $k$ be a field and let $X$ be a finite-type
$k$-scheme. Consider the three conditions

* (classical) $X\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is smooth in the earlier
  local-standard-smooth convention
  ([[def-smooth-morphism-classical]], [[def-smooth-morphism-to-field-classical]]);
* (scheme) $X\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is smooth in the scheme-theoretic sense of
  [[def-smooth-morphism-schemes]];
* (regular) every local ring $\mathcal O_{X,x}$ is a regular local ring.

1. Conditions (classical) and (scheme) are equivalent for every field $k$,
   closed points or not.
2. If moreover $k$ is perfect, then all three conditions are equivalent.
3. Consequently, for $k$ perfect, a classical smooth $k$-variety in the earlier
   convention (finite type over $k$, and irreducible or reduced if that
   convention so requires) has smooth structure morphism $X\to\operatorname{Spec}k$;
   conversely a reduced finite-type $k$-scheme with smooth structure morphism is
   classically smooth at every point and all its local rings are regular.
4. Irreducibility and connectedness are not consequences: the disjoint union of
   two copies of the affine line is finite type, reduced and scheme-smooth over
   $k$, but is neither irreducible nor connected. Those properties belong to the
   definition of "variety" and must be imposed separately.

No hypothesis of reducedness, irreducibility or separatedness is used in the
equivalences of clauses 1 and 2.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $f:X\to S$ be a morphism locally of
finite presentation ([[def-locally-finite-presentation-morphism]]) and let
$x\in X$ with $s=f(x)$. Then $f$ is smooth at $x$
([[def-smooth-morphism-schemes]]) if and only if there are affine open
neighbourhoods $U=\operatorname{Spec}C$ of $x$ and
$V=\operatorname{Spec}A$ of $s$ with $f(U)\subseteq V$ and a presentation of
$C_h$, for some $h\in C\smallsetminus\mathfrak q$ with $\mathfrak q$ the prime
of $x$, as
$$C_h\;\cong\;\Bigl(A[t_1,\dots,t_m]/(f_1,\dots,f_r)\Bigr)_g,$$
in which some $r\times r$ minor of the Jacobian matrix
$\bigl(\partial f_j/\partial t_i\bigr)$ has image a unit of $C_h$. Such a chart
is flat over $A$ with geometrically regular fibres whose components have
dimension $m-r$; in the local-dimension convention of
[[def-relative-dimension-smooth-morphism]] it exhibits relative dimension
$m-r$ at $x$.

The criterion demands that *some* presentation have an invertible $r\times r$
minor; it does not demand this of an arbitrary redundant equation list, and
$r>m$ makes an invertible $r\times r$ minor impossible by definition of the
matrix shape.

Let $m,n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb C^m\times\mathbb C^n$ be open, let
$f:U\to\mathbb C^n$ be holomorphic, and let $(a,b)\in U$ satisfy $f(a,b)=0$.
Assume the complex Jacobian with respect to the second block is invertible:

Then there are neighbourhoods $A$ of $a$ and $B$ of $b$, and a unique

$$f(z,\varphi(z))=0\qquad(z\in A),$$

and, after shrinking $A\times B$ if needed,

$$f(z,w)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad w=\varphi(z).$$

an affine chart $X_0$ of $X$ — and a nonempty affine open subvariety
$W\subseteq Y_{\mathrm{reg}}$ — a nonempty principal open of an affine chart
of $Y$ — such that:

1. $f(V)\subseteq W$, and $V\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ and
   $W\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ are smooth, so that $V$ and $W$ are smooth
   affine classical varieties over $k$;
2. the restriction $f|_V\colon V\to W$ is a morphism of finite type and is
   smooth in the sense of [[def-smooth-morphism-classical]]: it is locally
   standard smooth at every point of $V$; consequently the restriction
   $f|_V\colon V\to Y$ (equivalently $V\to Y_{\mathrm{reg}}$) is smooth as
   well.

In particular $f$ is smooth at every point of the nonempty open subset $V$ of
its source. Neither $X$ nor $Y$ is assumed smooth outside its regular locus,
and the target-side statement — a dense open subset of $Y$ over which the
source is smooth — is *not* asserted here: it requires a smooth source and
fails without that hypothesis.

Assume the Axiom of Choice (AC). Let $f:X\to S$ be a morphism locally of
finite presentation ([[def-locally-finite-presentation-morphism]]) and let
$\operatorname{Sm}(f)\subseteq X$ be its smooth locus
([[def-smooth-locus-morphism]]). Then $\operatorname{Sm}(f)$ is an open subset
of $X$, and the restriction of $f$ to this open subset is a smooth morphism.

Let $k$ be algebraically closed. The closed-point construction and its inverse
whose points are the nonempty irreducible closed subsets (with each original point identified with its singleton) give an
equivalence between irreducible classical $k$-varieties (which have a finite
affine cover by definition) and integral finite-type $k$-schemes satisfying
the affine-overlap separation condition.

Let $F:M^m\to N^n$ be smooth and let $Z\subseteq N$ be an embedded submanifold
of codimension $c$. If $F\pitchfork Z$, then $F^{-1}(Z)$ is an embedded
submanifold of $M$ of codimension $c$. For each $p\in F^{-1}(Z)$,

$$ T_pF^{-1}(Z)=\{v\in T_pM:dF_p(v)\in T_{F(p)}Z\}. $$

Let $X$ be a topological space. Its **fundamental groupoid**
$\Pi_1(X)$ is the following category ([[def-category]]).

- The objects are the points of $X$.
- A morphism $x\to y$ is an endpoint-fixed path-homotopy class $[\alpha]$
  of paths $\alpha:[0,1]\to X$ with $\alpha(0)=x$ and $\alpha(1)=y$, in
  the sense of [[def-homotopy-relative-and-path-homotopy]].
- If $\alpha:x\to y$ and $\beta:y\to z$, composition is
  $$[\beta]\circ[\alpha]=[\alpha*\beta].$$
  Thus the path written first is traversed first, while the categorical
  composite has the usual right-to-left notation.
- The identity at $x$ is the class of the constant path $c_x$, and the
  inverse of $[\alpha]$ is the reversed path class $[\bar\alpha]$.

The endpoint-fixed concatenation calculations in
[[thm-fundamental-group-laws]] prove that composition is independent of
representatives, associative, and unital, and that reversal gives a two-sided
inverse. Hence every morphism is an isomorphism, so this category is a
groupoid.

No connectedness, local connectedness, basepoint, or universal cover is part
of the definition. If $X=\varnothing$, both its object and morphism classes are
empty. A one-point space still has all of its endpoint-fixed loop classes;
contractibility is not inserted into the definition.

Let $X$ be a locally path-connected topological space
([[def-locally-connected]]). Then:

1. **Path components are open**, hence clopen, hence unions of them are clopen.
2. **Components and path components agree**: $P(x) = C(x)$ for every $x \in X$
   ([[def-path-connected]], [[def-connected-component-and-quasicomponent]]).
3. **If $X$ is moreover connected ([[def-connected-space]]) then $X$ is
   path-connected.**

Claim 3 is the statement in the title; claims 1 and 2 are what carry it, and both
are worth having on their own. Local path-connectedness alone does not make a
space path-connected — a two-point discrete space is locally path-connected and
is not path-connected — so the connectedness hypothesis in claim 3 is not
removable.

Throughout, $I := [0,1] = \{\, t \in \mathbb{R} : 0 \le t \le 1 \,\}$
([[def-interval]]) carries the subspace topology inherited from $\mathbb{R}$ with
its usual topology ([[def-subspace-topology-top]],
[[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]], [[def-metric-topology]],
[[def-metrizable-space]]). It is called the **unit interval**.

Let $X$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]) and let
$x, y \in X$.

- A **path in $X$ from $x$ to $y$** is a continuous map $\gamma : I \to X$
  ([[def-continuous-map-top]]) with $\gamma(0) = x$ and $\gamma(1) = y$. Its
  **image** is $\gamma[I]$.
- $X$ is **path-connected** when for every pair $x, y \in X$ there is a path in
  $X$ from $x$ to $y$. A subset $A \subseteq X$ is a **path-connected subset**
  when the space $A$ with its subspace topology is path-connected; equivalently,
  when any two of its points are joined by a path whose image lies in $A$, by the
  characteristic property of a map into a subspace
  ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]).
- Write $x \sim y$ when a path in $X$ from $x$ to $y$ exists. The **path
  component** of $x$ is its equivalence class
  $$P(x) \;:=\; \{\, y \in X : x \sim y \,\} .$$
- The empty space is path-connected, the defining condition quantifying over no
  pair of points, and so is every one-point space, the constant path joining its
  point to itself.

**$\sim$ is an equivalence relation on $X$, and the obligation is discharged
here**, so that "equivalence class" above denotes.

*Reflexive.* The constant map $\gamma(t) = x$ is continuous, every preimage being
$\varnothing$ or $I$ ([[def-continuous-map-top]]), and joins $x$ to $x$.

*Symmetric.* If $\gamma$ joins $x$ to $y$, put $\bar\gamma(t) := \gamma(1-t)$.
The map $r : I \to I$, $r(t) = 1 - t$, is continuous: for $s, t \in I$ one has
$|r(s) - r(t)| = |s - t|$, so a ball of radius $\varepsilon$ around $r(t)$ pulls
back to contain the ball of radius $\varepsilon$ around $t$
([[def-metric-ball]], [[def-metrizable-space]]). Hence
$\bar\gamma = \gamma \circ r$ is continuous ([[lem-continuity-is-local-and-pastes]],
claim 1) and joins $y$ to $x$.

*Transitive.* Let $\gamma_1$ join $x$ to $y$ and $\gamma_2$ join $y$ to $z$.
Define $\delta : I \to X$ by

$$\delta(t) \;:=\; \begin{cases} \gamma_1(2t), & 0 \le t \le 1/2, \\ \gamma_2(2t - 1), & 1/2 \le t \le 1. \end{cases}$$

The two clauses agree at $t = 1/2$, both giving $\gamma_1(1) = y = \gamma_2(0)$,
so $\delta$ is a well-defined function. The sets $[0,1/2]$ and $[1/2,1]$ are
closed in $I$ and cover it, and there are **two** of them, so the finite closed
form of the pasting lemma applies ([[lem-continuity-is-local-and-pastes]],
claim 3). On $[0,1/2]$ the map $\delta$ is $\gamma_1 \circ a_1$ with
$a_1(t) = 2t$, and on $[1/2,1]$ it is $\gamma_2 \circ a_2$ with
$a_2(t) = 2t - 1$; each $a_k$ is continuous into $I$, since
$|a_k(s) - a_k(t)| = 2|s-t|$, so the ball of radius $\varepsilon/2$ around $t$
maps into the ball of radius $\varepsilon$ around $a_k(t)$
([[def-metric-ball]], [[def-metrizable-space]],
[[def-subspace-topology-top]]). So both restrictions are continuous by
[[lem-continuity-is-local-and-pastes]] claim 1, hence $\delta$ is continuous, and
it joins $x$ to $z$.

**The path components partition $X$**, being the classes of an equivalence
relation, and each is a path-connected subset of $X$: two points of $P(x)$ are
joined to $x$, hence to each other by the transitivity construction above, and
the resulting path has image inside $P(x)$: if $\delta$ is a path from $x$ and
$s \in I$, then $t \mapsto \delta(st)$ is a path from $x$ to $\delta(s)$,
continuous because $t \mapsto st$ satisfies $|st_1 - st_2| \le |t_1 - t_2|$ and
is therefore continuous into $I$ by the ball criterion used above, so every point
of the image is itself joined to $x$.

derivations.claim: Charts and path-connected neighbourhoods. The regular local rings of $S$ are domains by [F7]. The minimal-prime correspondence shows that only one irreducible component passes through any point; the finitely many components are therefore disjoint and both closed and open. Connectedness leaves one component. We may consequently view $S$ as an integral finite-type separated scheme by the classical-scheme equivalence in [F7]; smoothness of the algebraic variety means every local ring is regular, so by the equivalence of [F7] the structure morphism $S\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb C$ is scheme-smooth. Fix $x\in S$. Applying the Jacobian criterion of [F7] to this morphism gives an affine neighbourhood of $x$ with a presentation $C_h\cong(\mathbb C[t_1,\dots,t_m]/(f_1,\dots,f_r))_g$ in which some $r\times r$ minor of the Jacobian matrix $(\partial f_j/\partial t_i)$ is invertible at $x$, and whose fibres have dimension $m-r$; here the fibre is the local variety itself, so its chart dimension is $m-r$, and the nonempty-open dimension equality of [F7] gives $m-r=n=\dim S$. If $r=0$ the chart is already open in affine space. For $r>0$, after relabelling the coordinates and applying the holomorphic implicit function theorem of [F7] (adding an unused parameter if the free-coordinate block is empty) to the holomorphic map $(f_1,\dots,f_r)$ near the image of $x$, the common zero locus is locally the graph of a holomorphic function of the remaining $m-r=n$ coordinates; the graph coordinate map identifies a neighbourhood of $x$ in the analytic topology with an open ball in $\mathbb C^n$, and this analytic topology is the one of [F7]. The same presentation and implicit-function argument applied to the reduced induced structure of a locally closed smooth complex subvariety exhibits its points as complex charts of dimension equal to its complex dimension. Consequently $S$, and every smooth locally closed complex subvariety of $S$, is a complex manifold for the analytic topology, hence in particular a smooth real manifold of twice its complex dimension; the chart balls are path-connected neighbourhoods, so $S$ and its open subsets are locally path connected.

Smoothing a based loop. Let $\gamma:S^1\to S$ be a continuous based loop. Choose a continuous surjection $\psi:S^1\to S^1$ with $\psi(*)=*$ that is constant on a neighbourhood of $*$: in angular coordinates it is induced by a nondecreasing surjection $\lambda:[0,1]\to[0,1]$ constant at $0$ and $1$ on endpoint collars. The interpolation $(1-u)t+u\lambda(t)$ descends to a homotopy from the identity fixing $*$; then $\gamma_1=\gamma\circ\psi$ is a continuous based loop, constant on an open arc $W_0\ni*$ where $\gamma_1= s$, and it is based-homotopic to $\gamma$. The map $\gamma_1$ is smooth (indeed constant) on an open neighbourhood of the closed set $A=\{*\}$, so the relative Whitney approximation of [F5] applies: there are a smooth based loop $\gamma_2:S^1\to S$ and an open neighbourhood $W$ of $*$ such that $\gamma_2=\gamma_1$ on $W$ and $\gamma_1$ is homotopic to $\gamma_2$ by a homotopy fixed on $W$. Thus $\gamma_2$ is a smooth based loop, equal to $\gamma_1=s$ on the open neighbourhood $W\cap W_0$ of the base point, with $[\gamma_2]=[\gamma_1]=[\gamma]$ in $\pi_1(S,s)$.

A finite decomposition of the complement into codimension-two smooth pieces. The complement $Z=S\setminus U$ is closed and proper, and $S$ is irreducible by step 1.1. We construct pairwise disjoint smooth locally closed complex subvarieties $(Z_j)$ covering $Z$, each of complex dimension at most $n-1$, by downward induction on dimension. Every irreducible component $C$ of $Z$ is a proper closed irreducible subvariety of the irreducible $S$, so $\dim C\le n-1$: append $S$ to any chain of irreducible closed subsets of $C$ to obtain a chain one term longer in $S$, using the chain-dimension definition in [F7]. The same argument gives the dimension drop for every proper closed subset of an irreducible component below. Suppose a closed algebraic subset $T\subseteq Z$ is given in which every irreducible component has dimension at most $d$. For each irreducible component $C$ of $T$ of dimension exactly $d$, the regular locus $C_{\mathrm{reg}}$ is a nonempty Zariski open subset of $C$: the generic-smoothness corollary of [F7], applied to the constant morphism from the irreducible classical variety $C$ to a point, produces a nonempty open subset of the regular locus, which is open by [F7]. The sets $C_{\mathrm{reg}}\setminus\bigcup_{C'\ne C}C'$, for the finitely many top-dimensional components $C$, are pairwise disjoint smooth locally closed complex subvarieties of dimension $d$. What they do not cover of $T$ is the union of the lower-dimensional components, the singular loci of the top-dimensional components, and the intersections of a top-dimensional component with another component; the lower-dimensional components have dimension at most $d-1$ by assumption and the other sets are proper closed subsets of top-dimensional irreducible components, hence have dimension at most $d-1$ by the chain argument, so the leftover $T'$ is a closed algebraic subset all of whose components have dimension at most $d-1$. Iterating from $T=Z$ and $d=n-1$ produces finitely many disjoint smooth locally closed pieces, and the iteration stops at dimension $0$, where the pieces are points and nothing is left over. Each piece has complex dimension at most $n-1$, so its real dimension is at most $2n-2$ and its real codimension in the smooth real manifold $S$ of step 1.1 is at least two; being a smooth locally closed complex subvariety, each piece is an embedded submanifold of $S$.

A cutoff vanishing at the base point and equal to one over the bad set. Let $\gamma_2$ be the smooth loop of step 1.2, denoting by $\gamma_2^{-1}(Z)\subseteq S^1$ the compact bad set. If it is empty, then $\gamma_2$ already lies in $U$ and its class is represented in $U$; assume it is nonempty. Since $\gamma_2$ equals the constant $s\in U$ on the open neighbourhood $W_2=W\cap W_0$ of $*$, the compact set $K=\gamma_2^{-1}(Z)$ is disjoint from $W\cap W_0$. Choose an open arc $W'\ni*$ with $\overline{W'}\subseteq W_2$, put $U_1=S^1\setminus\overline{W'}$ and $U_2=W_2$; these open sets cover $S^1$, and $K\subseteq S^1\setminus W_2\subseteq U_1$. By the partition-of-unity theorem [F4] applied to the cover $\{U_1,U_2\}$ choose a subordinate smooth partition of unity $(\chi_1,\chi_2)$ and set $\chi=\chi_1$. Then $\chi$ is smooth with values in $[0,1]$, equal to $1$ on the open set $S^1\setminus\operatorname{supp}(\chi_2)\supseteq S^1\setminus W_2\supseteq K$, and equal to $0$ on the open set $S^1\setminus\operatorname{supp}(\chi_1)\supseteq S^1\setminus U_1=\overline{W'}\ni*$; moreover whenever $\chi(p)=0$ we have $\chi_2(p)=1$, so $p\in\operatorname{supp}(\chi_2)\subseteq W_2$ and hence $\gamma_2(p)=s\in U$. In particular $\chi(*)=0$.
The truncated perturbation family is transverse to every piece. Apply the perturbation lemma

A parameter outside all bad sets, and surjectivity. For each piece $Z_j$ of step 2.1 the set $N_j\subseteq B$ of parameters $a$ with $\widetilde{\mathcal F}_a$ not transverse to $Z_j$ is null by the parametric transversality theorem [F2]. Since there are finitely many pieces, the union $N=\bigcup_jN_j$ is null in the positive-dimensional smooth manifold $B$ by [F6], so its complement is dense by [F6] and in particular nonempty; choose $a\in B\setminus N$. Then the slice $\widetilde{\mathcal F}_a:S^1\to S$ is a smooth based loop transverse to every $Z_j$. A transverse map from a one-dimensional manifold cannot meet a piece of real codimension at least two: if $\widetilde{\mathcal F}_a(p)\in Z_j$, transversality would give $\dim T_{\widetilde{\mathcal F}_a(p)}S\le\dim\operatorname{im}(d(\widetilde{\mathcal F}_a)_p)+\dim T_{\widetilde{\mathcal F}_a(p)}Z_j\le1+(2n-2)<2n$, a contradiction. Hence $\widetilde{\mathcal F}_a(S^1)$ meets no $Z_j$ and therefore lies in $U$. The map $(p,u)\mapsto\widetilde{\mathcal F}(p,ua)$, $0\le u\le1$, is a homotopy from $\gamma_2$ to $\widetilde{\mathcal F}_a$ through based loops, so $[\widetilde{\mathcal F}_a]=[\gamma_2]=[\gamma]$ in $\pi_1(S,s)$ by [F8], while $[\widetilde{\mathcal F}_a]$ lies in the image of $\pi_1(U,s)\to\pi_1(S,s)$ by [F8]. In the discarded case $K=\varnothing$ of step 2.2 the loop $\gamma_2$ itself already lies in $U$, so the same conclusion holds. Since every class in $\pi_1(S,s)$ has a continuous based loop representative, the map $\pi_1(U,s)\to\pi_1(S,s)$ is surjective.

Path connectedness. Let $x,y\in U$. The chart balls of step 1.1 make $S$ locally path connected, so connectedness and [F9] give a continuous path $\beta$ from $x$ to $y$; reparametrize it to be constant near its endpoints. Traverse $\beta$ on the first quarter of $S^1$, its reverse on the second quarter, and the constant path at $x$ on the second half. This gives a continuous circle map constant near all junctions. Apply [F5] to this circle map, relative to the finite closed set of junctions, to obtain a smooth loop equal to the original on neighbourhoods of those junctions. Its bad set is disjoint from those neighbourhoods. Repeat step 2.2 with $W_2$ the union of these constant neighbourhoods and $W'$ a smaller union with closure in $W_2$. The same two-set partition supplies a cutoff vanishing near all junctions, equal to one near the bad set, and with every zero lying where the loop is in $U$. Steps 3.1 and 4.1 then give a perturbed loop in $U$ agreeing with the original near the junctions. Its first quarter joins $x$ to $y$ in $U$. Thus $U$ is path connected; when $Z=\varnothing$ the unperturbed path already suffices.

boundaries.evidence: If $n=0$ then $S$ is a point, $Z=\varnothing$ and $U=S$; the discarded case $K=\varnothing$ of step 4.1 proves surjectivity and step 5.1 the path-connectedness criterion (steps 4.1, 5.1).
Dimension zero and the empty complement are exactly the cases handled in step 4.1's $K=\varnothing$ branch and step 5.1; no positive-dimensional parameter count is needed there.
For a one-dimensional base $S$, $Z$ is finite and the strata of step 2.1 are points, of real codimension two in the surface $S$; steps 2.2-5.1 apply verbatim.

The complement $Z$ may be empty, reducible, singular or of mixed dimension; step 2.1 iterates the dimension descent using only generic smoothness of components, and step 4.1 discards the empty bad set.
The cutoff fixes the basepoint in steps 2.2–4.1. Step 5.1 fixes both path endpoints by smoothing a circle map relative to all junctions.

AC supplies countable choice for approximation, partitions and transversality, and supplies the assumptions of the regular-local, dimension, generic-smoothness and classical-scheme inputs in F7. (Statement; steps 1.1–4.1.)

boundaries.reason: The lemma asserts path-connectedness and surjectivity, not a biconditional; no forward iff direction is owed.
No converse is asserted.

template_review.reason: Statement starts with a nonempty Zariski open in a connected smooth algebraic variety and concludes path connectedness and fundamental-group surjectivity. The proof perturbs loops away from the complement; surjectivity is not asserted to characterize algebraic open inclusions.

risk_review.notes: Read seven proof steps, all thirty actual dependency interfaces and the tubular-perturbation construction. Checked regular-local-domain component disjointness, finite smooth complement decomposition including lower-dimensional components, codimension at least two, angular based smoothing, cutoff zeros via the other partition function, transversality of parameter directions and radial homotopy, and endpoint-fixed path smoothing on a circle. AC supplies all algebraic and countable-choice hypotheses. Empty complement and n=0 give U=S and need no parameter selection. The tubular construction chooses its proper embedding through thm-weak-whitney-proper-embedding-theorem, whose actual Statement specifies R^(2n+1), hence positive parameter dimension even for a point. An initially proposed qualification was unnecessary and reverted before handoff. No claim changed, all current mathematical risks resolved.

citations.quote:
Let $A$ be a finite-dimensional algebra over a field and let $J=J(A)$. Then
$J$ is nilpotent, and the quotient algebra $A/J$ is semisimple.

Let $A$ be a finite-dimensional associative $\mathbb C$-algebra with unit, and let
$(\cdot,\cdot):A\times A\to\mathbb C$ be the **trace form**
$$(a,b):=\operatorname{tr}(L_{ab}),$$
where $L_c:A\to A$ is left multiplication by $c$, $L_c(x)=cx$, and the trace is
that of [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. Then:

1. $(\cdot,\cdot)$ is a symmetric associative bilinear form:
$(a,b)=(b,a)$ and $(ab,c)=(a,bc)$ for all $a,b,c\in A$;
2. $(\cdot,\cdot)$ is nondegenerate if and only if $A$ is semisimple
([[def-semisimple-ring]]);
3. if $A$ is semisimple, then either $A=0$ or
$A\cong\prod_{i=1}^r\operatorname M_{d_i}(\mathbb C)$ with $r\ge1$, $d_i\ge1$,
the simple left $A$-modules are the natural $d_i$-dimensional modules of the
factors ([[thm-simple-modules-over-semisimple-rings]]), and under such an
isomorphism the trace form corresponds to
$$((X_i),(Y_i))\longmapsto\sum_{i=1}^r d_i\,\operatorname{tr}(X_iY_i),$$
a sum of nondegenerate matrix trace pairings. No statement of this item uses the
Axiom of Choice.

Let $R$ be a nonzero unital ring. Then $R$ is semisimple if and only if $$R\cong\prod_{i=1}^rM_{n_i}(D_i)$$ for positive integers $r,n_i$ and division rings $D_i$. See [[thm-endomorphism-ring-of-the-left-regular-module-is-opposite]].

Let $r\ge1$, let every $n_i\ge1$, let every $D_i$ be a division ring, and put $R=\prod_{i=1}^rM_{n_i}(D_i)$. Then every simple left $R$-module is supported on exactly one factor and is isomorphic to that factor's column module $D_i^{n_i}$. These column modules give all simple left $R$-module isomorphism classes, with one class for each factor. See [[thm-wedderburn-artin-theorem]].

For a finite-length module, the direct-sum, sum-of-simples, and complement characterizations of semisimplicity are equivalent without any choice principle. See [[thm-equivalent-characterizations-of-semisimple-modules]].
A left $R$-module is **semisimple** when it is an internal direct sum of simple submodules, allowing the empty direct sum. Hence the zero module is semisimple.

For a left $R$-module $M$, the **socle** is $$\operatorname{Soc}(M):=\sum\{S\le M:S\text{ is simple}\}.$$ Concretely it is the submodule generated by the union of all simple submodules. If there are none, the sum is $0$, so the definition is always meaningful.

derivations.claim: Identify the radical of the regular trace form with $J$. The ideal $J$ is nilpotent and $B/J$ is semisimple, by [F1]. Choose a composition series of the left regular $B$-module; the simple factors are killed by $J$, since $JS=S$ for a simple factor would give $J^kS=S$ for every $k$, contradicting nilpotence. Each simple type of $B/J$ occurs among these factors: $B/J$ is a quotient of $B$, so its left regular module is a quotient of the regular module and its composition factors, namely $d_i\ge1$ copies of each column module, occur in the series. In a basis adapted to the series the diagonal blocks of $L_b$ are the factor actions, so $\operatorname{tr}(L_b)=\sum_im_i\operatorname{tr}(\overline b_i)$ with multiplicities $m_i\ge1$. Therefore the radical $\{b:(b,c)=0\text{ for all }c\}$ of the trace form is exactly $J$: it contains $J$, and on $B/J$ the induced form is the sum over $i$ of $m_i$ times the nondegenerate matrix trace pairing of the factor $M_{d_i}(\mathbb C)$, which is nondegenerate because $m_i\ne0$ and $\mathbb C$ has characteristic zero, by [F2].

Descend the kernel to a rational subspace. Evaluate the trace form in the rational basis $a_1,\dots,a_d$ of $A$: the Gram matrix $T=(\operatorname{tr}(L_{a_ia_j}))_{i,j}$ has rational entries, because each $L_{a_ia_j}$ is the extension to $\mathbb C$ of the rational endomorphism of $A$ given by left multiplication by $a_ia_j$, and the trace of such an extension is the trace of a rational matrix. By step 1.1 its kernel in $B$ is $J$. Let $J_0=\{a\in A:Ta=0\}\subseteq A$ be the kernel computed in $\mathbb Q$-coordinates, a rational subspace; then $J_0\otimes\mathbb C=J$, since a rational linear system has the same solutions after extension of scalars and its solution space over $\mathbb C$ is the complexification of its rational solution space. Since $J$ is a two-sided ideal of $B$, the intersection $J_0=J\cap A$ is a two-sided ideal of $A$, and $W=\{v\in V:J_0v=0\}$ is a rational $A$-submodule of $V$.

Identify $W_{\mathbb C}$ with the socle. Because $J_0\otimes\mathbb C=J$, one has $W_{\mathbb C}=\{v\in V_{\mathbb C}:Jv=0\}$: choose a finite rational basis $j_1,\ldots,j_a$ of $J_0$, so $W$ is the kernel of $V\to V^a$, $v\mapsto(j_1v,\ldots,j_av)$. Write an element of $V_{\mathbb C}$ as $\sum_{i=1}^k v_i\otimes\lambda_i$ with the finitely many $\lambda_i$ rationally independent, obtained by reducing the span of its original coefficients. The equations $j_a\sum_i v_i\otimes\lambda_i=0$ imply $j_av_i=0$ for each $a,i$, by comparing coordinates in a finite rational basis of the span of the vectors $j_av_i$. Thus it lies in $W\otimes\mathbb C$; the reverse inclusion is immediate. No basis of an infinite-dimensional space is selected. Every simple $B$-submodule $S\subseteq V_{\mathbb C}$ is killed by $J$: otherwise $JS=S$, and then $J^kS=S$ for all $k$, contradicting nilpotence of $J$. Hence the socle of $V_{\mathbb C}$ is contained in $\{v:Jv=0\}$. Conversely $\{v:Jv=0\}$ is a module over the semisimple algebra $B/J$, and it is a sum of simple modules: for each of its vectors $v$, the cyclic module $(B/J)v$ is a quotient of the regular $B/J$-module, and that regular module is a finite direct sum of the column modules of [F2], so its image is a sum of simple modules. Each cyclic module is finite-dimensional, so [F3] makes its sum of simple images a finite direct sum. Every vector of $\{v:Jv=0\}$ therefore belongs to a sum of simple $B$-submodules, and this annihilator, containing every simple submodule, is exactly the socle. This argument does not require $V$ to be finite-dimensional. Thus the socle of $V_{\mathbb C}$ equals $W_{\mathbb C}=W\otimes\mathbb C$, a rational $A$-submodule complexified.

boundaries.evidence: For $V=0$ the socle is zero, and step 3.1 identifies it with $W\otimes\mathbb C$ for the rational subspace $W=0$; the nonvanishing clause has empty hypothesis (statement).
The zero module is included in step 3.1 and its socle is $0$; step 4.1 covers exactly the nonzero case for the nonvanishing assertion.
For nonzero rank-one V the unital action gives W=V by step 4.1; step 3.1 also handles arbitrary-dimensional V through its finite cyclic submodules.

The algebra $B$ may have nonzero radical, so $V_{\mathbb C}$ need not be semisimple; step 1.1 identifies the radical of the trace form with $J$ and step 3.1 uses the annihilator of $J$, with no separability or reducedness assumed.

boundaries.reason: No interval or asymptotic parameter occurs. The algebra is finite-dimensional; the module V may have arbitrary dimension.

boundaries.evidence: No choice is used: step 1.1 builds one composition series by choosing successive minimal positive dimensions, and steps 1.1-2.1 solve rational linear systems (steps 1.1, 2.1).

boundaries.reason: The statement is not a biconditional: it asserts rational descent of the socle and a nonvanishing implication.
No converse direction is asserted.

template_review.reason: Statement constructs a rational submodule W whose complexification is the socle and proves nonvanishing when V is nonzero. The trace-kernel construction is one-direction rational descent, rather than a criterion characterizing rational algebras from descended socles.

risk_review.notes: Read all four steps and all seven cited interfaces, including the full regular-trace and finite-length supplier proofs. Positive composition multiplicities make the quotient trace pairing nondegenerate in characteristic zero; rational kernel extends to the radical. Checked annihilator scalar extension by finite rationally independent coefficients, infinite-dimensional V via finite cyclic modules, zero V, rank one, and nonzero radical via its last nonzero power. The proof needs no basis of arbitrary V or arbitrary choice. The full socle need not equal the sum of minimum-dimensional simples; current Source notes preserve that distinction. Historical finite-dimension mismatch and source identification are repaired; no unresolved finding.

citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Every projective morphism in the finite-dimensional
H-projective convention of this page is proper: if $f:X\to S$ factors over $S$
as
$$X\xrightarrow{i}\mathbb P^n_S\longrightarrow S$$
with $n\ge0$, $i$ a closed immersion and the second arrow the projection, then
$f$ is proper. The empty source, the empty base and the case $n=0$ are
included, and no Noetherian, field, reducedness or nonemptiness hypothesis is
imposed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), inherited from the
Jacobian-criterion, ample-powers, Chern-form and comparison suppliers below.
Let $X$ be a smooth projective complex scheme of pure dimension $n\ge0$.

Then the closed points of $X$ carry a structure of **complex manifold**
$X^{\mathrm{an}}$, its **analytification**: if $X\ne\varnothing$ and $n\ge1$
this is a compact Hausdorff second-countable smooth complex manifold of complex
dimension $n$
([[def-complex-manifolds-and-holomorphic-vector-bundles]]); if $n=0$ it is the
finite discrete set $X(\mathbb C)$ with its unique complex structure in the
convention of
[[def-compact-kahler-manifold-and-hodge-polarization-conventions]]; and if
$X=\varnothing$ then $X^{\mathrm{an}}=\varnothing$. Every standard smooth
algebraic chart of $X$ becomes a holomorphic chart of $X^{\mathrm{an}}$, and
more generally, every morphism between smooth separated finite-type complex schemes of pure dimensions induces a holomorphic map between their analytifications. These analytifications are constructed by the same charts and need not be compact; separatedness and finite type ensure that they are Hausdorff and second-countable.

Moreover, for every ample invertible sheaf $A$ on $X$ there is a smooth
positive closed real $(1,1)$-form $\eta_A$ on $X^{\mathrm{an}}$ whose de Rham
class is the real image of the topological first Chern class
$c_1(A):=c_1(A^{\mathrm{an}})\in H^2(X^{\mathrm{an}};\mathbb Z)$:
$$J_{X^{\mathrm{an}}}[\eta_A]=\rho_{X^{\mathrm{an}}}\bigl(c_1(A)\bigr),$$
where $J$ is the de Rham comparison and $\rho$ the change of coefficients
$\mathbb Z\to\mathbb R$
([[lem-rational-cohomology-scalar-comparison-for-compact-smooth-manifolds]]).
In dimension $n=0$ and for $X=\varnothing$ every $2$-form and every degree-two
cohomology class is zero and $\eta_A=0$, so the identity holds trivially.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $f:X\to S$ be a morphism locally of
finite presentation ([[def-locally-finite-presentation-morphism]]) and let
$x\in X$ with $s=f(x)$. Then $f$ is smooth at $x$
([[def-smooth-morphism-schemes]]) if and only if there are affine open
neighbourhoods $U=\operatorname{Spec}C$ of $x$ and
$V=\operatorname{Spec}A$ of $s$ with $f(U)\subseteq V$ and a presentation of
$C_h$, for some $h\in C\smallsetminus\mathfrak q$ with $\mathfrak q$ the prime
of $x$, as
$$C_h\;\cong\;\Bigl(A[t_1,\dots,t_m]/(f_1,\dots,f_r)\Bigr)_g,$$
in which some $r\times r$ minor of the Jacobian matrix
$\bigl(\partial f_j/\partial t_i\bigr)$ has image a unit of $C_h$. Such a chart
is flat over $A$ with geometrically regular fibres whose components have
dimension $m-r$; in the local-dimension convention of
[[def-relative-dimension-smooth-morphism]] it exhibits relative dimension
$m-r$ at $x$.

The criterion demands that *some* presentation have an invertible $r\times r$
minor; it does not demand this of an arbitrary redundant equation list, and
$r>m$ makes an invertible $r\times r$ minor impossible by definition of the
matrix shape.

Let $m,n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb C^m\times\mathbb C^n$ be open, let
$f:U\to\mathbb C^n$ be holomorphic, and let $(a,b)\in U$ satisfy $f(a,b)=0$.
Assume the complex Jacobian with respect to the second block is invertible:

$$\det\left(\frac{\partial f_j}{\partial w_k}(a,b)\right)_{1\le j,k\le n}\ne0.$$

Then there are neighbourhoods $A$ of $a$ and $B$ of $b$, and a unique
holomorphic map $\varphi:A\to B$, such that

$$f(z,\varphi(z))=0\qquad(z\in A),$$

and, after shrinking $A\times B$ if needed,

$$f(z,w)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad w=\varphi(z).$$

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open and let
$F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be smooth. For every base point $(t_0,x_0)\in D$ there are
$h>0$ and an open neighbourhood $W$ of $(t_0,x_0)$ such that each initial pair
$(s,y)\in W$ has a unique solution on $[s-h,s+h]$, and the resulting local
solution map is smooth in the initial time and initial state.

Let $F(t,x,\lambda)$ be jointly $C^\infty$ in $(t,x,\lambda)$ on an open time-state-parameter
domain. Near any base data $(t_0,x_0,\lambda_0)$ there are a compact time
interval $I$ and a neighbourhood $W$ of $(x_0,\lambda_0)$ such that, for every
$(y,\lambda)\in W$, the solution of

$$x'(t)=F(t,x(t),\lambda),\qquad x(t_0)=y,$$

is defined on $I$, and the resulting solution map is smooth in the pair
$(y,\lambda)$.

Let $V:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be a smooth vector field on an open set $U$, and for
each $x_0\in U$ let $x(\,\cdot\,;x_0)$ denote the unique maximal solution of
$x'=V(x)$ with $x(0)=x_0$. Then the maximal solution domain

$$\Omega:=\{(t,x_0)\in\mathbb R\times U:t\text{ lies in the maximal interval of }x(\,\cdot\,;x_0)\}$$

is open in $\mathbb R\times U$. On $\Omega$, the evaluation map
$\Phi(t,x_0):=x(t;x_0)$ is smooth in the state variable and continuous jointly in
$(t,x_0)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $M$ be a closed smooth
manifold ([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Then $M$ has the homotopy type of a finite
CW complex ([[def-cw-complex-with-closure-finiteness-and-weak-topology]]).

Assume AC. For a CW pair $(X,A)$ and local system $\mathcal L$, the cellular cochain complex obtained from the skeletal filtration computes singular cohomology with local coefficients:
$$H^n\bigl(C^*_{\mathrm{cell}}(X,A;\mathcal L)\bigr)\cong H^n(X,A;\mathcal L).$$
For a connected pair, it is the equivariant-Hom complex on cellular chains after the published right chain action is converted to the left action $g\cdot c=c\cdot g^{-1}$; equivalently its cochains satisfy $\varphi(c\cdot g)=g^{-1}\varphi(c)$. The comparison is natural for cellular maps with correctly directed coefficient morphisms.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $X$ be a metric space
([[def-metric-space]]) having a neighbourhood basis of contractible open sets at
every point, and let $k$ be a field. Write $k_X$ for its constant sheaf. There
are natural isomorphisms
$$H^q(X,k_X)\cong H^q_{\operatorname{sing}}(X;k)$$
in every degree, where the left side is derived cohomology in the category of
sheaves of $k$-vector spaces (computed with the functorial $k$-linear injective
resolutions supplied by
[[lem-ringed-space-module-sheaves-enough-injectives]]; compare
[[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]]). The same assertion holds on
every open subset of $X$. In particular a nonempty contractible space with this
local property has constant-sheaf cohomology $k$ in degree zero and zero
otherwise. This applies to every finite-polyhedral open star and to its
nonempty intersection with a closed simplex.

Assume AC and the actual geometric and derived-incidence suppliers of the Verdier theorem. For analytic algebraic maps on its proved constructible subcategory, the six operations $f^*,Rf_*,Rf_!,f^!,\otimes_k^L,R\mathcal Hom$ have their three adjunctions, composition and identity comparisons, ordinary proper and extraordinary proper base change, projection formula, support localization, dualizing transitivity and trace. The comparisons commute with Cartesian pasting, composition of maps, evaluation and trace, giving a coherent pull-push product calculus. For a locally trivial product projection with finite-type smooth fibre $F$, the actual finite product cochain model gives $R\mathrm{pr}_*\mathrm{pr}^*B\simeq B\otimes_k C^*(F;k)$, with its ordinary unit. Smooth base change for $Rf_*$ holds whenever a supplied factorization $f=p\circ j$ has $p$ proper and $j$ an open inclusion with the conical local models below; proper maps already satisfy it. Their finite constructible models commute with extension of coefficient fields. Geometric output preservation is the exact geometric supplier, not an additional axiom.

Assume AC. For a compact Kähler manifold $X$ in the sense of
[[def-compact-kahler-manifold-and-hodge-polarization-conventions]], every de
Rham class has a unique smooth harmonic representative and
$$H^k(X;\mathbb C)=\bigoplus_{p+q=k}H^{p,q}(X),\qquad \overline{H^{p,q}(X)}=H^{q,p}(X).$$
Here $H^{p,q}(X)$ is precisely the set of classes with a $d$-closed smooth
representative of type $(p,q)$, so the decomposition is independent of the
Kähler metric. Writing $\Omega_X^p$ for the sheaf of holomorphic $p$-forms (the
kernel of $\bar\partial$ on the sheaf $\mathcal A^{p,0}$ of smooth $(p,0)$-forms),
$H^{p,q}(X)$ is isomorphic to $H^q(X,\Omega_X^p)$, the sheaf cohomology of
[[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]]. The Hodge filtration
$F^a=\bigoplus_{p\ge a}H^{p,k-p}$ of $H^k(X;\mathbb C)$ equals the filtration
induced by the holomorphic-degree filtration of the de Rham complex, whose
spectral sequence has $E_1^{p,q}=H^q(X,\Omega_X^p)$ and degenerates at $E_1$.
Pullback by holomorphic maps of compact Kähler manifolds and cup product
preserve Hodge type, so $H^k(X;\mathbb Q)$ is a functorial rational pure Hodge
structure.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M,E,P$ have exactly the compact, boundaryless, scalar-positive-symbol and formal symmetry hypotheses of [[thm-elliptic-differential-operators-on-compact-vector-bundles-have-parametrices-and-regularity]], with $\operatorname{dom}P=H^2(M,E)$. Write $\mathcal H=\ker P$.

Then $\mathcal H$ is finite dimensional and consists of smooth sections, $\operatorname{ran}P=\mathcal H^\perp$ is closed in $L^2$, and
$$L^2(M,E)=\mathcal H\mathbin{\oplus^\perp}\operatorname{ran}P.$$
Let $\Pi$ be the orthogonal projection onto $\mathcal H$. There is a unique linear operator $G:L^2\to H^2\cap\mathcal H^\perp$ with
$$PG=I-\Pi\quad\hbox{on }L^2,\qquad GP=I-\Pi\quad\hbox{on }H^2,\qquad G\Pi=\Pi G=0.$$
It is bounded from $H^k$ to $H^{k+2}$ for every integer $k\ge0$, compact and selfadjoint on $L^2$, and preserves smooth sections. For all such $k$,
$$H^k=\mathcal H\oplus P(H^{k+2}),\qquad C^\infty(M,E)=\mathcal H\oplus P(C^\infty(M,E)),$$
where the second summands are the corresponding intersections with $\mathcal H^\perp$, and the decompositions are topological. The projection is smoothing: for every integer $r\ge0$, $\|\Pi f\|_{C^r}\le C_r\|f\|_2$. Consequently $G$ is a two-sided parametrix with finite-rank smoothing remainders. If additionally $(Pu,u)_2\ge0$ for smooth $u$, then $P$ and $G$ are nonnegative on their respective domains.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), inherited from the
analytic suppliers below. Let $X$ be a compact Kähler $n$-fold in the
conventions of
[[def-compact-kahler-manifold-and-hodge-polarization-conventions]], with
Kähler form $\omega$, and let $0\le k\le n$. For this proof also write $Q_k$ for the same form on all of $H^k$, and on the primitive space $P^k$ put
$$Q_k(a,b)=\epsilon(k)\int_Xa\wedge b\wedge\omega^{n-k},$$
where $a,b$ are closed smooth representatives of the classes and the integral
is independent of the representatives. This form is $(-1)^k$-symmetric, pairs
$P^{p,q}$ only with $P^{q,p}$, and for nonzero $a\in P^{p,q}$ satisfies
$$i^{p-q}Q_k(a,\bar a)=(n-k)!\,\|a_{\mathrm{harm}}\|_{L^2}^2>0.$$
If $[\omega]=\ell\in H^2(X;\mathbb Q)$, then $Q_k$ is a rational polarization
of $P^k$, and full $H^k$ is polarized by the orthogonal direct sum form $S_k$
that on $L^rP^{k-2r}$ is $(-1)^rQ_k$, equivalently
$S_k(L^ru,L^rv)=Q_{k-2r}(u,v)$ for $u,v\in P^{k-2r}$; degrees $k>n$ are
polarized by transporting the polarization of $H^{2n-k}$ along $L^{k-n}$, with
Tate shift. For every real Kähler class the same positivity and nondegeneracy
statements hold, without rationality. In particular this applies to smooth
closed complex projective submanifolds of projective space with a hyperplane
polarization, hence to smooth projective complex varieties through their smooth
projective analytifications; more generally it applies to every real Kähler
class, including $\ell+\epsilon\eta$ when represented by a positive closed
form. For any continuous family of Kähler classes the primitive kernels (of
every fixed degree $0\le k\le n$) vary continuously as subspaces; rational
primitive spaces are asserted only at rational classes.
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every open cover of a smooth manifold admits a smooth partition of unity subordinate to it.

Assume AC. Let $R$ be a commutative PID and $X,Y$ spaces such that every $H_q(Y;R)$ is a finite free $R$-module. For every $n\ge0$ the additive singular cohomology cross product gives an isomorphism
$$\bigoplus_{p+q=n}H^p(X;R)\otimes_RH^q(Y;R)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }H^n(X\times Y;R).$$
All indices are nonnegative. The symmetric assertion holds when every $H_p(X;R)$ is finite free instead. No bound on the number of nonzero homology degrees and no finite-rank hypothesis on the singular chain groups is required.

Fix a commutative unital ring $R$. A **left $R$-module local system** on a
space $X$ is a covariant functor
$$\mathcal L:\Pi_1(X)\longrightarrow R\text{-}\mathbf{Mod},$$
where the source is [[def-fundamental-groupoid-of-a-space]], functor means
[[def-functor-and-contravariant-functor]], and the target is the category in
[[prop-modules-and-homomorphisms-form-category-rmod]]. Write
$\mathcal L_x$ for its value at $x$ and
$$T_\gamma=\mathcal L([\gamma]):\mathcal L_x\longrightarrow\mathcal L_y$$
for transport along a path $\gamma:x\to y$. Every arrow of the source has a
reversed inverse, so functoriality makes every $T_\gamma$ an isomorphism, with
$T_{\bar\gamma}=T_\gamma^{-1}$ and
$T_{\alpha*\beta}=T_\beta T_\alpha$.

A **morphism of local systems** $\eta:\mathcal L\to\mathcal K$ is a natural
transformation ([[def-natural-transformation]]): it is a family of
$R$-linear maps $\eta_x:\mathcal L_x\to\mathcal K_x$ satisfying
$$\eta_yT^\mathcal L_\gamma=T^\mathcal K_\gamma\eta_x$$
for every path $\gamma:x\to y$. Isomorphisms of local systems are natural
isomorphisms.

A continuous map $f:X\to Y$ induces a functor
$\Pi_1(f):\Pi_1(X)\to\Pi_1(Y)$ by $x\mapsto f(x)$ and
$[\gamma]\mapsto[f\gamma]$. Postcomposition preserves constants, reversals,
and concatenation, so this is well defined. The **pullback local system** is
$$f^*\mathcal K=\mathcal K\circ\Pi_1(f),\qquad (f^*\mathcal K)_x=\mathcal K_{f(x)},\qquad T^{f^*\mathcal K}_\gamma=T^\mathcal K_{f\gamma}.$$
Pullback of a coefficient morphism is defined componentwise. Thus
$(gf)^*=f^*g^*$ and $1_X^*$ are literal equalities of functors with these
conventions.

All definitions work independently on every path component. The empty space
has the unique empty local system. No basepoint, universal cover, common fiber,
or choice principle is required.

For later comparison with group rings, if $x$ is fixed and
$g=[\alpha]\in\pi_1(X,x)$, the base fiber is given the **left monodromy
convention**
$$g\cdot m:=T_{\bar\alpha}(m).$$
The reversal is essential: covariance and first-path-first multiplication give
$T_{\alpha*\beta}=T_\beta T_\alpha$, so
$T_{\overline{\alpha*\beta}}=T_{\bar\alpha}T_{\bar\beta}$, exactly the left
action law $(gh)m=g(hm)$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be Banach spaces over the same scalar field
([[def-banach-space]]).

1. If $R\in\mathcal B(X)$ satisfies $\|R\|<1$
   ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]], [[def-operator-norm]]), then $I-R$ is
   invertible with inverse the operator-norm limit of the partial sums
   $\sum_{n<N}R^n$, the norm limit being taken in
   $\mathcal B(X)$ ([[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]), and
   $$\Bigl\|\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}R^n\Bigr\|\le\frac{1}{1-\|R\|}.$$
2. If $A\in\mathcal B(X,Y)$ is invertible with $A^{-1}\in\mathcal B(Y,X)$ and
   $E\in\mathcal B(X,Y)$ satisfies $\|A^{-1}E\|<1$, then $A+E$ is invertible
   with $(A+E)^{-1}=\bigl(I+A^{-1}E\bigr)^{-1}A^{-1}\in\mathcal B(Y,X)$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]) carrying the product topology of $n$
copies of the usual topology of $\mathbb{R}$ ([[def-product-topology]]), and let
$d_2$ be the Euclidean metric. Then:

1. The product topology on $\mathbb{R}^n$ **is** the metric topology of $d_2$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]), so $\mathbb{R}^n$ as a product and $\mathbb{R}^n$ as
   a metric space are one topological space, and it is metrizable
   ([[def-metrizable-space]]).
2. A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset for the product
   topology ([[def-compact-space]]) **if and only if** $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}^n$ and bounded ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its three metrics only there; for $n = 0$ the product is a
one-point space and is compact. **No choice principle is used**: the metric
statement it is read off from is proved by bisection
([[thm-heine-borel-rn]]).

For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]) and every family
$(X_k)_{k < n}$ of compact topological spaces ([[def-compact-space]],
[[def-topological-space]]), the product

$$\prod_{k < n} X_k$$

with the product topology ([[def-product-topology]]) is compact. In particular a
binary product $X \times Y$ of compact spaces is compact, and the empty product,
a one-point space, is compact.

**No choice principle is used beyond [[lem-finite-choice]]**, which is a theorem
of ZF. That is what separates the finite case from the arbitrary one, where the
Axiom of Choice is genuinely spent.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Assume countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $F:M\to N$ be continuous, let $A\subseteq M$ be closed, and suppose $F$ is smooth on an open neighbourhood of $A$. Then there exist a smooth map $\widetilde F:M\to N$ and an open neighbourhood $W$ of $A$ such that $\widetilde F=F$ on $W$ and $F$ is homotopic to $\widetilde F$ by a homotopy fixed on $W$, hence relative to $A$. No compactness of $A$ or its neighbourhood is assumed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). If $U$ is a nonempty
Zariski open subset of a connected smooth complex algebraic variety $S$, then
$U$ is path connected and $\pi_1(U,s)\to\pi_1(S,s)$ is surjective for every
$s\in U$ ([[def-fundamental-groupoid-of-a-space]]).
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Every metric space is paracompact.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. If $X$ is paracompact and Hausdorff and
$\mathcal U$ is an open cover, there are a set $S$, a map $s\mapsto U_s$ from
$S$ into $\mathcal U$, and locally finite open covers $\{V_s\}_{s\in S}$ and
$\{W_s\}_{s\in S}$ with
$$\overline{V_s}\subseteq W_s\subseteq\overline{W_s}\subseteq U_s\quad(s\in S).$$

Let $\mathcal F$ be a presheaf on a topological space $X$. For every $x\in X$,
the sheafification map induces a bijection
$$\eta_{\mathcal F,x}:\mathcal F_x\xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }(a\mathcal F)_x.$$

Let $\mathcal J$ be a small filtered category
([[def-filtered-category-and-filtered-colimit]]). The filtered colimit functor
$$\operatorname*{colim}_{\mathcal J}:\mathbf{Ab}^{\mathcal J}\to\mathbf{Ab}$$
on abelian groups is exact ([[def-exact-functor-between-abelian-categories]]).
Equivalently:

1. for a $\mathcal J$-indexed diagram of short exact sequences
   $0\to A_j\to B_j\to C_j\to 0$ of abelian groups, the colimit sequence
   $$0\to\operatorname*{colim}_jA_j\to\operatorname*{colim}_jB_j\to\operatorname*{colim}_jC_j\to 0$$
   is short exact;
2. for a $\mathcal J$-indexed diagram of cochain complexes of abelian groups
   $K_j^\bullet$, the canonical map
   $\operatorname*{colim}_jH^p(K_j^\bullet)\to H^p(\operatorname*{colim}_jK_j^\bullet)$
   is an isomorphism for every $p\in\mathbb Z$; in particular the colimit of a
   diagram of exact complexes is exact in every degree.

Let $H:X\times I\to Y$ be a homotopy from $f$ to $g$. Then the prism operator
$P_H$ of [[def-prism-operator-for-a-homotopy]] satisfies
$$g_\#-f_\#=\partial P_H+P_H\partial$$
as homomorphisms $C_n(X;G)\to C_n(Y;G)$ for every $n\geq 1$ and every abelian
group $G$. In degree $0$, the same identity reduces to
$$g_{\#,0}-f_{\#,0}=\partial P_H:C_0(X;G)\to C_0(Y;G).$$

The inclusion $C_\bullet^{\mathcal U}(X;G)\hookrightarrow C_\bullet(X;G)$
induces an isomorphism on homology.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. If $R$ is a PID, $F$ is a free $R$-module, and
$N\subseteq F$, then $N$ is free (with no finite-rank assumption on $F$).

Assume the Axiom of Choice, and let $X$ be a topological space. Then
$\mathrm{Ab}(X)$ has enough injectives, every abelian sheaf on $X$ admits an
injective resolution ([[def-injective-resolution-in-an-abelian-category]]), and
the embeddings below supply one injective resolution datum
([[def-supplied-injective-resolution-datum]]) on the whole category
$\mathrm{Ab}(X)$: for every abelian sheaf $\mathcal F$ the datum assigns one
specific injective resolution
$$0\to\mathcal F\to I^0(\mathcal F)\to I^1(\mathcal F)\to\cdots,$$
built functorially from $\mathcal F$ with no further selection.

Let $j:U\hookrightarrow X$ be the inclusion of an open subspace.

1. For every sheaf of abelian groups $\mathcal F$ on $U$ and every sheaf of
   abelian groups $\mathcal G$ on $X$, there is a natural bijection
   $$\operatorname{Hom}_X(j_!\mathcal F,\mathcal G) \cong \operatorname{Hom}_U(\mathcal F,j^{-1}\mathcal G).$$
2. The functor $j_!$ is exact on sheaves of abelian groups.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X$ be a topological space and let
$$0\to\mathcal F\to\mathcal G\xrightarrow{\ \varphi\ }\mathcal H\to0$$
be a short exact sequence of abelian sheaves on $X$
([[def-exact-sequence-sheaves]]) in which $\mathcal F$ is flasque
([[def-flasque-sheaf]]).

1. For every open subset $U\subseteq X$ the map
   $\varphi_U:\mathcal G(U)\to\mathcal H(U)$ is surjective.
2. If moreover $\mathcal G$ is flasque, then $\mathcal H$ is flasque.

The Axiom of Choice is used exactly once, to apply Zorn's lemma in part 1
([[thm-zorn]], [[cor-ac-iff-zorn]]).

Assume the Axiom of Dependent Choice.

Let $\mathcal A$ and $\mathcal B$ be abelian categories, let $I$ be supplied
injective resolution data on all objects of $\mathcal A$, and let
$F:\mathcal A\to\mathcal B$ be an additive left exact functor. Then the additive functors
$$R_I^nF:\mathcal A\to\mathcal B,\qquad n\geq 0,$$
admit connecting maps that make them into a cohomological delta functor on
$\mathcal A$, and $R_I^0F$ is naturally isomorphic to $F$.

Assume the Axiom of Dependent Choice.

Let $I$ be a supplied injective resolution datum on a class $\mathcal D$ and
$F:\mathcal A\to\mathcal B$ an additive functor between abelian categories.
If $J\in\mathcal D$ is an injective object, then for every $n>0$,
$$R_I^nF(J)=0.$$

Assume the Axiom of Dependent Choice.

Let $I$ be a supplied injective resolution datum on a class $\mathcal D$, let
$F:\mathcal A\to\mathcal B$ be an additive left exact functor, and let
$$0\to A\to J^0\to J^1\to J^2\to\cdots$$
be an $F$-acyclic resolution of $A$ relative to $I$. Assume moreover that
$A\in\mathcal D$ and that, for $Z^0:=A$ and
$$0\to Z^q\to J^q\to Z^{q+1}\to0\qquad(q\ge0),$$
each $Z^q$ lies in $\mathcal D$. Then for every $n\ge 0$ there is a canonical
isomorphism
$$R_I^nF(A)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }H^n(F(J^\bullet_{\mathrm{del}})).$$

Let
$$0\to A^\bullet\to B^\bullet\to C^\bullet\to0$$
be a short exact sequence of cochain complexes in an abelian category. Then
there is a natural exact sequence
$$\cdots\to H^n(A)\to H^n(B)\to H^n(C)\xrightarrow{\partial^n}H^{n+1}(A)\to H^{n+1}(B)\to H^{n+1}(C)\to\cdots.$$

Every finitely generated abelian group $G$ has unique canonical decompositions

$$G\cong\mathbb Z^r\oplus\mathbb Z/(n_1)\oplus\cdots\oplus\mathbb Z/(n_t),\qquad 1<n_1\mid\cdots\mid n_t,$$

and

$$G\cong\mathbb Z^r\oplus\bigoplus_{p,j}\mathbb Z/(p^{e_{p,j}}),$$

where $r$ and the finite torsion data are unique up to the stated order. The torsion summand is finite. The trivial group has $r=0$ and empty torsion data.

derivations.claim: Analytic submersion and properness. The relative projective embedding is a closed immersion $X\hookrightarrow S\times\mathbb P^N$. Its analytification is closed because the defining polynomial equations are continuous. For each compact $K\subset S^{\mathrm{an}}$, the inverse image $f^{-1}(K)$ is a closed subset of $K\times\mathbb P^N(\mathbb C)$ and is compact: projective space is the continuous image of the unit sphere in $\mathbb C^{N+1}$, which is compact by [F12]. The finite-product assertion in [F12] makes $K\times\mathbb P^N$ compact. Thus $f^{\mathrm{an}}$ is topologically proper, in addition to algebraic properness from [F1]. The smooth Jacobian presentation and holomorphic implicit function theorem [F2] give local holomorphic submersion coordinates (with no equations there is nothing to solve, and an unused parameter handles a zero-dimensional free block). The smooth quasiprojective source and base are Hausdorff second-countable complex manifolds; they are metrizable as locally closed subspaces of projective space. Each fibre is a compact smooth projective complex manifold, possibly empty or with components of different dimensions, and [F1] supplies a Kähler form on each component.

Integral sheaf comparison. We supply the coefficient extension that [F4] states only for fields. On a metric space $M$ with a contractible-open basis let $\mathcal C^q$ be the sheafification of integer-valued singular cochains. The shrinking argument of [F11] makes every section over an open set $V$ the germ of a global cochain: choose a locally finite refinement $W_i$ with closure in a representative neighbourhood, assign to each simplex contained in some $W_i$ one representative value, and assign zero otherwise. At any point only finitely many $W_i$ can intervene; their representative germs agree on a smaller neighbourhood, so this assignment has the required germ. Consequently every $\mathcal C^q$ is flasque. The stalk complex of $\mathbb Z_M\to\mathcal C^\bullet$ is exact: stalk preservation, exact filtered colimits and contraction of cofinal contractible neighbourhoods in [F11] give $\mathbb Z$ in degree zero and zero in higher degrees. These flasque terms are acyclic for abelian sheaf cohomology: injectives are flasque by the extension-by-zero adjunction, and embedding a flasque sheaf into an injective leaves a flasque quotient with surjective section map, by [F11]; dimension shifting in the derived long exact sequence proves positive acyclicity. The acyclic-resolution theorem therefore applies. Finally the kernel of $C^*(M;\mathbb Z)\to\Gamma(M,\mathcal C^\bullet)$ is the directed union of cochains vanishing on the small simplices of a cover. For each cover, the quotient of all integer chains by small chains is a complex of free abelian groups, since small simplices are a subset of the basis; it is acyclic by the small-chain theorem [F11]. Its boundaries are free by the PID submodule theorem [F11], so its short exact cycle-boundary sequences split by lifting bases, making it contractible. Its integer dual is thus acyclic. Directed union and the cochain long exact sequence give the natural comparison $H^q(M,\mathbb Z_M)\cong H^q_{\mathrm{sing}}(M;\mathbb Z)$. The canonical augmentation and sheafification maps commute with pullback, so the comparison is natural and applies also to open subspaces.

Transport and the cohomology local systems. Choose a smooth horizontal complement to $\ker df^{\mathrm{an}}$ on $X^{\mathrm{an}}$ (locally the product charts of step 1.1 provide one; glue the local choices with a smooth partition of unity on the manifold $X^{\mathrm{an}}$ [F9]). For a smooth path $\gamma:[0,1]\to S$ and a point $x\in f^{-1}(\gamma(0))$, the horizontal ODE $\dot x(t)\in H_{x(t)}$ with $f(x(t))=\gamma(t)$ has a unique maximal solution by [F3]; because $f$ is proper, the lifted solution stays in the compact set $f^{-1}(K)$ for a compact neighbourhood $K$ of $\gamma([0,1])$, so it exists on all of $[0,1]$: local ODE existence neighbourhoods cover the compact time-state set $[0,1]\times f^{-1}(K)$, and a finite subcover gives a common positive continuation interval; a finite maximal endpoint would therefore admit continuation, contradicting maximality. The resulting transport map $\tau_\gamma:f^{-1}(\gamma(0))\to f^{-1}(\gamma(1))$ is a diffeomorphism, smooth in the initial point by the smooth dependence on initial data in [F3], and an endpoint-fixed smooth homotopy of paths gives a homotopy of terminal diffeomorphisms by the parameter dependence in [F3]. The terminal point maps need not be identical, but their induced maps on cohomology are identical by homotopy invariance. Smooth representatives and homotopies suffice for the fundamental groupoid by [F10]: reparametrize paths to be constant near endpoints and extend them constantly to $\mathbb R$, then apply relative Whitney approximation fixing those collars. For a homotopy between smooth representatives, reparametrize both variables to have constant collars, extend to $\mathbb R^2$ by clamping the variables, and approximate relative to the boundary collars, where the map is smooth. This produces a smooth homotopy with the prescribed endpoints and boundary paths. Concatenation and reversal give composition and inverses of the cohomology transports. The assignments $x\mapsto H^m(f^{-1}(x);R)$ for $R=\mathbb Z,\mathbb Q$, together with the covariant isomorphisms $T_\gamma=(\tau_\gamma^{-1})^*:H^m(f^{-1}(\gamma(0));R)\to H^m(f^{-1}(\gamma(1));R)$, therefore define functors on the fundamental groupoid of $S$, that is, $R$-module local systems in the sense of [F8]; this is the local system $R^mf^{\mathrm{an}}_*\underline R$ of the family.

Cohomology sheaves and lattices. The horizontal transport of step 2.1 along radial paths in a small convex base chart $B$ gives a smooth trivialization $f^{-1}(B)\cong B\times F$, with inverse furnished by reversed paths and smooth dependence from [F3]. For $R=\mathbb Z,\mathbb Q$, the stalk of $R^mf_*\underline R$ is $\operatorname*{colim}_{B\ni s}H^m(f^{-1}(B),\underline R)$: a flasque resolution computes direct image because its restriction to every inverse image of an open set is section-acyclic, as in step 1.2, and exact stalk colimits commute with cohomology. The comparisons of [F4] and step 1.2 identify these groups with singular cohomology. Contracting $B$ gives $H^m(B\times F;R)\cong H^m(F;R)$, compatibly with transport. Thus both higher direct images are the local systems of step 2.1. Finite CW type and cellular cochains [F4] make the fibre's integral cohomology finitely generated. The finite cellular cochain complex tensored with $\mathbb Q$ is the rational cellular cochain complex, and rational linear-system reduction gives $H^m(F;\mathbb Z)\otimes\mathbb Q\cong H^m(F;\mathbb Q)$. By [F11], quotienting integral cohomology by torsion gives a finite free full lattice; transport preserves torsion and hence this lattice.

Continuous Hodge decomposition. Use the fixed-fibre trivialization of step 3.1. An empty fibre contributes zero; its zero-dimensional components are finite sets with constant type $(0,0)$ and require no elliptic argument. Work separately on its positive-dimensional components for the following construction. The relative projective embedding restricts the Fubini–Study form to a smooth family of fibrewise Kähler metrics. On the fixed compact $F$ let $\Delta_t:H^2\to L^2$ be the corresponding Laplacians, using one reference metric for the Sobolev norms. Their coefficients vary continuously, so $\Delta_t-\Delta_0$ tends to zero in operator norm $H^2\to L^2$. Let $\Pi_0$ and $G_0$ be the harmonic projection and Green operator from [F6]; $\Delta_0+\Pi_0$ is invertible with inverse $G_0+\Pi_0$. The Neumann-series assertion of [F12] therefore gives continuous inverses $A_t^{-1}=(\Delta_t+\Pi_0)^{-1}$ for nearby $t$. On $\ker\Delta_t$, the map $\Pi_0$ is injective, because $(\Delta_t+\Pi_0)u=0$ would force $u=0$; by [F6] both harmonic kernels have the same dimension, the fixed Betti number, so this map is bijective. Thus $A_t^{-1}|_{\ker\Delta_0}$ is its inverse and identifies the kernels continuously. The same argument in $H^{k+2}\to H^k$, for every $k\ge0$, gives continuity in each Sobolev norm. The continuously varying type projections on forms commute with the Kähler Laplacians by [F6] (the type-preservation calculation in its Hodge-decomposition proof, step 2.1); restricted to these identified finite-dimensional harmonic spaces they are continuous idempotents, whose ranks are locally constant and whose images vary continuously. They give the subspaces $H_t^{p,q}$ under the harmonic/de Rham identification. The pure decomposition, conjugation symmetry and metric independence in [F6] consequently give the required continuous pure Hodge decomposition of weight $m$.

Flat Lefschetz operators and polarization. Let $L$ be a relatively ample line bundle on $X$. Its first Chern class lies in $H^2(X;\mathbb Q)$. Apply the positive Chern-metric construction of [F1] to the ample restriction on each compact fibre, extend that metric to a neighbourhood using the smooth trivialization of step 2.1, and shrink the base chart so vertical positivity persists by compactness. Relative to a fixed smooth reference metric on $L$, patch the logarithms of the local metric ratios with a smooth partition of unity pulled back from the base. On a fibre these base weights are constant, so the resulting Chern curvature is their positive convex combination; it is globally closed, represents $c_1(L)$ and restricts on every fibre to a Kähler form with rational class. No positivity in base directions is asserted. Then in the product chart the restrictions to the fibres induce one and the same class on the fixed model $F$ under the identifications $\tau_\gamma$ of step 2.1, because those identifications are induced by the homotopic family of inclusions of the fibres into $X$ and cohomology is homotopy invariant; explicitly, if $\psi_t:F\to f^{-1}(t)$ are the product-chart identifications, then the maps $(t,x)\mapsto\psi_t(x)$ exhibit the composites $i_t\circ\psi_t$ as homotopic to $i_s\circ\psi_s$, so $\psi_t^*(c_1(L)|_{f^{-1}(t)})=\psi_s^*(c_1(L)|_{f^{-1}(s)})$. Cup product and integration are compatible with the transport isomorphisms, so the map $a\mapsto c_1(L)\smile a$ is a flat Lefschetz operator, and the polarized Lefschetz decomposition supplied by [F7] is flat. The forms $Q_k$ of [F7] applied to the primitive pieces give a flat rational bilinear form, since their defining integrals involve only cup products, the flat powers of the Kähler class just described, and the constant sign $\epsilon(k)$; the positivity clause of [F7] holds on every fibre, and the full polarization is the sign-adjusted orthogonal sum along the flat Lefschetz decomposition, hence also flat, rational and positive. This supplies the flat rational polarization required in the definition.

Geometric closures and full lattices. All assertions are made over a fixed open piece of the base, and may be pulled back along a base change to any smooth $S'$ by change of the parameter. Products: for smooth projective $f_i:X_i\to S$, $i=1,2$, the product family $X_1\times_SX_2\to S$ is smooth projective, and the cohomological Künneth isomorphism of [F8] identifies $R^{m}(f_1\times_Sf_2)_*\mathbb Q$ with the direct sum of tensor products $R^pf_{1*}\mathbb Q\otimes R^{q}f_{2*}\mathbb Q$, $p+q=m$, compatible with Hodge type because pullback and wedge of $(p,q)$ forms preserve bidegree by [F6]; this rational comparison uses [F8] over the field $\mathbb Q$, where the finite-dimensional homology groups are free. The ambient product-family cohomology has a full stable integral lattice by step 3.1; intersecting it with each rational tensor summand gives a full monodromy-stable lattice in that summand, since a rational basis can be multiplied by common denominators into the ambient lattice. Thus products and their full lattices are geometric without assuming that the integral cohomology of every smooth projective fibre is torsion-free. Direct sums in the same cohomological degree are realized by disjoint unions of families over $S$; different degrees are combined by the finite-sum realization clause of the definition. The degree-two cohomology of the constant family $\mathbb P^1\times S\to S$ is $\mathbb Q(-1)$, of type $(1,1)$, and its rational Hodge dual is $\mathbb Q(1)$, of type $(-1,-1)$, by the dual and Tate conventions in the definition. For a realization $H|_U\subseteq\bigoplus_i R^{m_i}(f_i)_*\mathbb Q(r_i)$, twisting by any integer $r$ gives the realization inside $\bigoplus_i R^{m_i}(f_i)_*\mathbb Q(r_i+r)$, which is allowed directly by that definition; the same rational idempotent remains flat and preserves the shifted Hodge types. Thus all integer Tate twists have the stated geometric realizations, without identifying a positive twist with untwisted degree-two cohomology. For a pure variation of weight $w$, its flat rational nondegenerate polarization of step 5.1 gives $H^*\cong H(w)$ as Hodge variations, so the just-proved Tate realization also realizes the dual; the dual of a full stable lattice is again full and stable. Finite sums of pure weights are handled componentwise. Exterior powers are Hodge direct summands of tensor powers cut out by the rational alternating idempotent, which is flat and a Hodge morphism on every fibre; more generally a prescribed flat rational idempotent that is a Hodge morphism on every fibre cuts out a geometric Hodge direct summand of a realized variation. Intersecting such a rational direct summand with the full ambient lattice of step 3.1 gives its full monodromy-stable lattice: a rational basis of the summand can be cleared to integral vectors of the ambient lattice, and flatness of the summand makes the intersection monodromy-stable. Finally, for a morphism $g:X'\to X$ of smooth projective complex varieties, $g^*:H^m(X;\mathbb Q)\to H^m(X';\mathbb Q)$ preserves Hodge types by the pullback functoriality clause of [F6], so rational pullbacks between smooth projective fibres are morphisms of pure Hodge structures. This proves every closure and lattice clause of the statement concerning a single smooth projective family; the Gauss-Manin family itself is geometric and polarizable by steps 2.1-5.1.

Extension to the whole geometric category. For a geometric object on connected $S$, choose its realization open $U$. Steps 3.1–6.1 supply a full stable lattice and, in each pure weight, a flat rational polarization on $H|_U$. By [F10], $\pi_1(U,s)\to\pi_1(S,s)$ is onto, so the same lattice in $H_s$ and the same bilinear form are preserved by every monodromy operator on $S$; transport extends them to $S$. The polarization's Hodge orthogonality extends from $U$ by continuity, since a proper algebraic subset has no analytic interior: on an irreducible smooth chart a regular defining function is holomorphic, and vanishing on a ball forces it to vanish identically by its power series and continuation through overlapping charts. Thus $U$ is analytically dense. The extended bilinear form is nondegenerate, being flat, and its Weil-operator Hermitian form is continuous and nondegenerate everywhere. It is positive on $U$; its eigenvalues cannot cross zero, so it is positive on all of $S$. Restrictions to Hodge direct summands are nondegenerate by positivity and have the intersected full stable lattices. Applying this argument componentwise to finite sums of pure weights completes the closure, dual, lattice and polarization assertions for all geometric objects, not just the realization open. In particular steps 2.1–5.1 construct the stated Gauss–Manin variation and its integral lattice on every nonempty connected base component. Disconnected bases are treated componentwise and the assertions over an empty base are vacuous.
